opening.headline: Learn criteria for determining how setting the dimensionality and operation type of the embedding affects search performance and storage costs.
body: Even if you embed the same document, the results will vary depending on the settings. Increasing the dimension will result in larger vectors, which will require more storage space, and if you do not specify an operation type, the model will not be able to create vectors for the purpose of retrieval.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the effects of dimensionality and dimension reduction, why we need to distinguish between query and document task types, and the problems that arise when we do not distinguish between them. The goal is to view both settings as a matter of balancing accuracy and cost.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Describe the effects of dimensionality reduction and task typing
Allows you to distinguish between dimensional accuracy and storage cost trade-offs

screens.title: Two settings change performance and cost
screens.lead: Read about the changes that occur when you change just two settings in the same document. Consider which settings will affect cost and which settings will affect accuracy.

visual.alt: Diagram showing how two settings, dimension and operation type, affect storage cost and retrieval accuracy, respectively.

paragraphs: A team is creating in-house document search. As the number of documents increased, two concerns arose. One is that vector storage space increases rapidly, and the other is that the relevance of the results is lower than expected.

The first has to do with dimensions. Even if you embed the same document, the larger the dimension, the larger the vector, which increases storage space and search time. The second has to do with the type of work. The Gemini documentation explains that specifying the right task type ensures that the embedding is optimized for that task, resulting in better performance and accuracy.
However, the team does not have a standard for determining the two settings. In many cases, the default value is used. This lesson covers what the two settings change and on what basis to decide.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Reducing the dimension by half halves the storage cost. How much will accuracy be reduced? We check with actual measurements in class.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience calculating storage costs.

screens.title: Recall your experience calculating vector storage costs.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever calculated the cost of vector storage?
items.answer: Storage costs increase linearly with document count and dimension. Although it may seem small at first, once you have millions of documents, storage space and search infrastructure costs will greatly influence your choice. Let's do the calculation ourselves in this lesson.

items.prompt: Have you guessed at number of documents x dimensions x bytes per number?
items.answer: That multiplication is the basic equation for storage capacity. Assuming one number is stored in 4 bytes, a 3072-dimensional vector for 1 million documents is approximately 12.3 GB. If you know the formula, you can immediately estimate the effect of changing the dimension.

items.prompt: Have you ever felt that changing dimensions changes your search speed?
items.answer: Shorter vectors tend to make searches lighter because there are fewer numbers to compare. The Gemini paper also explains that smaller output dimensions can save storage space and increase computational efficiency for subsequent applications.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized our experience, let us first check the effects of dimensionality and dimension reduction.

screens.title: Dimensionality and dimensionality reduction
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the dimensionality of the embedding. You can see how the storage capacity and accuracy metrics change as the dimensionality decreases.

visual.alt: Graph with overlapping bars showing vector size by dimension and lines showing accuracy metrics.

stops.body: The default output of the Gemini embedding model is 3072-dimensional and is always normalized. It has the largest storage capacity. Assuming each number is 4 bytes, 1 million documents is approximately 12.3 GB. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large also has a default length of 3072.

The Gemini documentation states that dimensions 768, 1536, and 3072 are recommended. Decreasing it to 1536 halves the storage capacity to about 6.1GB. The MTEB values ​​presented in the document are virtually the same: 68.16 for 2048 dimensions and 68.17 for 1536 dimensions.

The 768 dimension has a storage capacity of about 3.1GB, a quarter of the default. The MTEB value is 67.99, which is almost the same as 1536 dimensions. The documentation explains that performance is not strictly proportional to the size of the embedding dimension, with lower dimensions giving similar values ​​to higher dimensions.

256 Dimensions has a storage capacity of about 1.0 GB, which is one-twelfth of the default. The MTEB value is 66.19, which is lower than 67.99 for 768 dimensions. This is the section where accuracy begins to decrease noticeably at the cost of a significant reduction in cost.

Dimension 128 has the smallest storage capacity, but its MTEB value drops significantly to 63.31. There are limits to the benefits of reducing dimensionality. The point at which we can reduce it must be determined by directly measuring it with our own data.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the dimension knobs, let's next look at how task type affects embedding.

screens.title: Task Type: Queries and Documents Embed Differently
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how queries and documents are separated and reduced by each vendor.

tabs.label: Why distinguish?
tabs.body:
Search is asymmetric between queries and documents. Queries are short and purposeful, and documents are long and informative. Embedding in the same way does not reflect differences in wording between short question and long answer documents.

The Gemini documentation explains that specifying a task type optimizes the embedding for that task, resulting in better performance and accuracy. In asymmetric operations such as search, the operation prefix is ​​added only to the query, and the document format is used for the document. Conversely, symmetric operations use the same format for queries and documents.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body:
For text input in `gemini-embedding-2`, we strongly recommend entering work instructions in the prompt.

**Search Query**: `task: search result | query: {content}`

**Document to be searched**: `title: {title} | text: {content}` (`title: none` if there is no title)

For question answering, fact checking, and code searching, the document format is the same, with only the query wording different. Symmetric tasks, such as classification or clustering, use the same format for queries and documents. `gemini-embedding-001` specifies the `task_type` parameters, such as `RETRIEVAL_QUERY` and `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT`.

tabs.label: Voyage
tabs.body:
Anthropic does not provide its own embedding model, but rather guides Voyage AI. Voyage's call to `embed()` specifies `input_type`.

When embedding a document, use `input_type="document"`, and when embedding a query, use `input_type="query"`. The two values ​​have different purposes and should not be mixed.

Additionally, the latest Voyage models have 1024 dimensions as standard, and you can also choose 256, 512, and 2048 dimensions. Because the task type and dimension are specified together in the same call, both settings can be checked at once.

tabs.label: Consistency is key
tabs.body:
The type of work is more important than how you use it consistently. The Gemini documentation explains that, for example, if a document is embedded in a format for classification, the query should follow the same classification format.

Additionally, the similarity task phrase is for semantic text similarity and should not be used in searches. You need to get into the habit of checking whether the format used when indexing and the format used when querying come from the same rule.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the rules for each type of work, we will explain the problems that arise when they are not followed.

screens.title: Explanation: When there is no distinction between inquiry and document work types.
screens.lead: An instructor steps you through diagnosing search quality issues for a team. Select the right arrow to go through errors, symptoms, causes, and corrections. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Situation: Query and document were embedded in the same way
steps.body: One team embedded the document in `title: {title} | text: {content}` format and embedded the query the same way as the document, without any prefix. Because the code works and produces results, it is difficult to notice that there is a problem.

steps.title: Symptom: Top results are less relevant
steps.body: The percentage of correctly answered documents ranking in the top ten for evaluation questions was lower than expected. Although there was a correct answer, there were many cases where the ranking was pushed back or the wrong document was put in front. These symptoms do not mean that your search index is wrong, but may be a sign that the settings you made when creating the embed are not aligned with your goals.

steps.title: Cause: The difference between short queries and long documents was not reflected.
steps.body: The query is short and the document is long, which is asymmetric. Without distinguishing between operation types, the model will not know whether the text it is embedding is sought or found. This does not result in a vector optimized for search purposes.

steps.title: Pitfall: Don't substitute another task type
steps.body: Sentence similarity formats are sometimes used in searches to specify the type of operation. The Gemini documentation states that this format should not be used for search, but only for semantic text similarity. Although the names seem similar, they are settings with different purposes.

steps.title: Proofreading: Use query format for queries and document format for documents.
steps.body: Search consistently applies query formats to queries and document formats to documents. If `gemini-embedding-2`, embed the query as `task: search result | query: {content}` and the document as `title: {title} | text: {content}`. For Voyage, specify `input_type` as `query` and `document`, respectively.

steps.title: Re-index and re-evaluate
steps.body: If the way you embed a document changes, you will need to recreate existing document vectors. This is because changing just the query side breaks the rule. Re-index and compare the rankings using the same evaluation questions to see improvements. The setup problem is closed with measurements like this. It is recommended that evaluation questions include questions with different wording.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the results of our settings, we will balance the two settings in the final screen.

screens.title: Dimensions are the handle of accuracy and cost
screens.lead: The first question, how do these two settings affect performance and cost, is answered with what we learned today.

paragraphs: Dimensions are the knob that trades off accuracy and cost. Reducing it reduces storage space and search costs, but accuracy begins to decrease as the amount of reduction increases. Looking at the measured values, there is little difference between the 1536 dimension and the 768 dimension, and there is a significant drop in the 128 dimension.

Job type is a setting for accuracy, not cost. Because queries and documents are asymmetric, they must be embedded in their respective formats, and the same rules must be consistently followed when indexing and querying.
Finally, don't forget to normalize again when directly reducing dimensionality. For both settings, it is safest to rely on measurements of our data rather than feelings.

In practice, whenever you change the settings, compare the rankings using the same set of evaluation questions, and record the reason for the change and the results. If you have a record, you can use the same criteria again when replacing models.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: The dimensions are determined by the measurements of our data, and the task types are specified consistently across queries and documents.

checks.intro: Consider the precautions regarding dimensionality reduction we just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The dimensions of text-embedding-3-large were reduced by directly cutting the vector instead of setting its dimensions. What to do?
options: Increase the dimension back to its original state
Match the length of the query and document
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Directly reduced vectors do not have length 1, so they need to be normalized again.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That treatment will not solve the problem. Think about what happens to the length of a vector if you cut it.
checks.explain: If the dimension is directly reduced, normalization must be performed again. This is because the length of the reduced vector is not 1.

wrong.1: Without normalization, the rank agreement between cosine and dot product may be broken.
wrong.2: Since the purpose of dimension reduction is to reduce costs, it is not right to return it.
wrong.3: Matching the length is not relevant to this processing.

checks.intro: Check the last question, recalling the diagnosis you saw in the explanation. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: When I searched by embedding the query and document in the same way, the relevance of the top results decreased. What is the appropriate cause and correction?
options: This is because I followed the instructions to use the similarity theft task type in the search.
Since the dimension is too small, the maximum dimension is always used.
Since the asymmetry between the query and the document is not reflected, each format is used.
Reduce the index because the number of documents is large.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. In asymmetric searches, each format must be used consistently in queries and documents.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That explanation doesn't fit. Recall how queries and documents are different and how your settings reflect this.
checks.explain: The query is short and the document is long, which is asymmetric. The query format must be consistently applied to queries and the document format to documents.

wrong.0: The Gemini document actually advises against using similarity theft types in searches.
wrong.1: As the dimension increases, the storage cost increases and the asymmetry problem remains.
wrong.3: There is no evidence that the number of documents is the cause.

glossary.def: The length of the embedding vector. Affects storage size and expressiveness.
By reducing the length of the vector, storage space and calculation amount are saved. If you reduced it yourself, you need to normalize it again.
This is a setting that specifies the embedding method according to the purpose of use, such as query, document, classification, or similarity.
Vector storage capacity scales proportionally with document count and dimension. Calculated as number of documents x dimension x bytes per number.

misconceptions.fact: After the point where the accuracy gain diminishes, the cost only goes up. In measurements, dimensions 1536 and 768 were almost identical.

misconceptions.myth: Reducing the dimension significantly reduces quality.
misconceptions.fact: Models trained using the Matryoshka method maintain much of their performance even when scaled down. However, if you reduce it too much, the decline will be large, so it must be determined by measurement.

misconceptions.myth: The task type is optional and has no effect.
misconceptions.fact: Specifying a task type optimizes it for that task and improves accuracy. If not specified or specified incorrectly, search quality may decrease.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Dimensions are the knob that trades off accuracy and cost.
Reducing the dimensionality makes storage and retrieval lighter, but accuracy limits must be checked by measurement.
Task types are specified consistently across queries and documents.
After directly reducing the dimension, normalization is performed again.
